The 600-year-old mystery of the Voynich manuscript may be one step closer to being solved, researchers discover an unusual detail

mystery

Express newspaper

21/10/2026 20:50

One of history's greatest mysteries may have an unexpected explanation. Researchers believe the reason no one has been able to decipher the Voynich Manuscript, a mysterious book created in the early 15th century, may be because its pages were bound in the wrong order.

For more than six centuries, the Voynich manuscript has puzzled linguists, historians, cryptographers and code experts from around the world.

The mysterious book, consisting of about 240 pages, contains nearly 38 words written in an unknown writing system called "Voynichese", as well as dozens of strange illustrations depicting plants, human figures and unexplained symbols.

Despite numerous efforts, no one has been able to determine with certainty what language the manuscript contains or what its message is.

But a new study suggests that the problem may not lie solely in the mysterious language.

According to researchers, the manuscript pages may have been placed in the wrong order during a later bookbinding process, making the text even more difficult to understand.

Statistical analysis reveals discrepancies between pages

To examine this hypothesis, the researchers used modern statistical analysis techniques, comparing parts of text on different pages.

The goal was to determine whether pages located next to each other have similarities in writing structure.

The results revealed something unusual.

Pages that actually come one after the other often have very low levels of statistical similarity.

In contrast, some parts of the text that are far apart exhibit considerable similarities.

According to the study's authors, this may indicate that some pages that are now separate were originally placed together.

If this hypothesis is confirmed, reconstructing the original order could aid in understanding the structure of the manuscript and, potentially, in efforts to decipher it.

"You can't understand a book if the pages are jumbled"

Dr. Lisa Davis, a researcher affiliated with the Medieval Academy of America and Simmons University, is one of the study's authors.

In an interview with Live Science, she explained that the discovery does not yet constitute a final solution to the mystery.

"It doesn't get us to a full translation yet, but it helps us make progress, because you can't make sense of a book if all its pages are jumbled up," Davis declared.

According to her, the way the manuscript is physically constructed can be as important as its content.

Researchers believe that a more detailed analysis of the book's structure could help understand the relationship between texts and illustrations.

What is the Voynich manuscript?

The Voynich Manuscript is considered one of the most mysterious books of the medieval period.

It is written on parchment, a material usually made from animal skin and widely used for manuscripts before the spread of paper.

Carbon dating of the parchment places the creation of the material in the early 15th century.

The earliest historical documents suggest that the manuscript may have been purchased by the Holy Roman Emperor, Rudolph II, more than a century after its creation.

Later, the book ended up in the hands of Polish antiquarian and book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, from whom it took its name.

In 1969, the manuscript became part of Yale University's rare book collection, where it remains today.

Its content has sparked much discussion, particularly due to the unfamiliar writing and illustrations that do not easily match other works from the same period.

From medicine to magic, theories about the book's content

Over the decades, various scholars have proposed numerous interpretations of the manuscript.

Some have suggested that it may contain information on traditional medicine, the use of herbs, and the preparation of medicines.

Others have hypothesized that the text is related to gynecology, sexuality, and methods of contraception.

There have also been theories that the manuscript may contain secret religious knowledge, pagan practices or magical formulas.

However, none of these interpretations has been widely accepted as a solution to the mystery.

The lack of an identifiable language and the inability to find a reliable translation system have meant that the manuscript remains undeciphered.

The new study proposes a different approach: before trying to understand the words, experts should determine whether the pages are placed in the correct order.

A detail in the handwriting raised suspicions

The new hypothesis arose during Dr. Davis' research into the number of people who had participated in writing the manuscript.

She noticed that the characteristics of the calligraphy varied from one page to the next in a way that didn't seem logical.

Instead of writing styles following a clear continuity, they seemed to alternate in a chaotic manner.

This prompted the researcher to take a closer look at the physical organization of the book.

"We don't know if we're dealing with a code, but the Voynich manuscript has some unusual characteristics in its physical structure," Davis explained.

One of the most interesting details is related to the illustrations.

According to her, in some cases a figure continues beyond the border of one page and appears on the other side, even though there are several more pages between the two parts.

This discrepancy may be an indication that the pages are not linked in the original order.

How were books bound during the Middle Ages?

To understand the hypothesis, researchers have analyzed traditional methods of medieval book production.

At that time, books were usually prepared by folding sheets of parchment in half.

Such a folded sheet was called a "bifolium", creating two sheets or four pages.

Usually, several bifoliums were placed one inside the other to form a group of sheets, known as a "quire".

In many cases, five bifoliums were joined into a single set, while several such sets were sewn together along the back to create the book.

But the study's authors suspect that the Voynich manuscript was not originally intended to be organized in this way.

According to them, the original structure may have been much different from what we see today.

The book may have been a collection of separate sheets

Dr. Davis and her co-author, Dr. Colin Layfield from the University of Malta, propose that the manuscript may have originally been a collection of individually folded sheets.

These units, known as “singulons,” may have been used separately, similar to small booklets.

According to this hypothesis, the original readers may have examined these parts one after the other, without the need for them to be bound into a single book.

The current form may have been created later, when an owner or copyist of the manuscript joined the leaves together without understanding their contents.

If the person who bound the book did not know the language of the text, he may have placed the pages in the wrong order.

This would explain why some writing styles change suddenly and why some illustrations seem to continue on pages that are now far apart.

"When you start to analyze it in the context of other unusual features of the manuscript, all of these problems get an explanation," Davis said.

According to her, the theory also explains the possibility that each copyist wrote a separate sheet, as well as cases where illustrations extend beyond the fold of the parchment.

A study that could change the direction of research

The findings have been published in the scientific journal "Digital Medievalist".

The authors hope that their hypothesis will prompt linguists and cryptography experts to reconsider previous analyses.

According to researchers, many attempts to decipher the manuscript have relied on the assumption that the pages are in their original order.

If this assumption is wrong, some of the conclusions drawn so far may need to be re-evaluated.

In the study, the authors express hope that this approach will open a new era of research on the Voynich manuscript.

However, they acknowledge that much work remains to be done before the initial ranking of pages is determined.

Water stains can reveal the original order

One of the next steps in the research is related to the analysis of large water stains found in several parts of the manuscript.

Dr. Davis believes these marks could provide important clues about how the sheets were laid out in the past.

When water seeps into a set of pages placed one on top of the other, it can create similarly shaped stains on adjacent sheets.

If the pages were saved in their original order, some of these spots should match.

But in the Voynich manuscript, water stains often do not match between pages that are now next to each other.

This could be another sign that the ranking has been changed.

Researchers hope that comparing the shapes of the spots will help them identify sheets that were once placed together.

In this way, it may become possible to partially reconstruct the original structure of the book.

Can the 600-year-old mystery finally be deciphered?

Although the new study presents an interesting explanation for some of the Voynich manuscript's strangest features, it does not yet prove that the pages were bound incorrectly.

Also, even if the original sequence is discovered, it does not necessarily mean that the mysterious language can be translated immediately.

However, a clearer structure of the text could give scholars new opportunities to analyze the repetition of words, the relationships between parts of the manuscript, and their connection to the illustrations.

For a book that has resisted attempts at decipherment for centuries, even such a discovery could constitute significant progress.

The Voynich Manuscript remains one of the greatest mysteries in written history, but researchers are now exploring a new possibility: perhaps, to understand its contents, they must first discover how the book was supposed to have been organized. /GazetaExpress/
